keeper.text: Shh, we're between shows. Well, shh-ish. This is the Gaiety Theatre.
It opened in 1900 and was designed by Frank Matcham, the man behind half the great theatres in Britain.
Red velvet, gold plaster, and a ghost or two, depending who you ask.

then.text: The Gathering is on the prom every summer now. The Roll goes round the three islands and comes home to the Gaiety, where it lives in the prompt corner, behind a lock. Not the old drawer.
Tynwald, the torches and the bells, all in one ledger. I could not have asked for a better cast.
The pages are on their way home. Go and see what the island has put up on the prom. The Reader will want a word. I will be along as soon as I have found my glasses.
You have been to all three islands and listened. Now the awkward bit: who had the pages? Be sure. The Casebook in your Fieldbook has the evidence.
Mr Halcrow, of course. I shall write him a very polite letter. In pencil, so it can be rubbed out if the pages arrive.
Ring something in St Helier. The Bell Captain at the church is expecting you. The Occupation and the Liberation want ringing out, and a Roll is no use if nobody can ring it.
Next the Jersey War Tunnels, out in the country above St Helier. Listen to the Historian there, properly. It is not a cheerful visit, and it should not be.
Now to the Guernsey Occupation Museum. The Volunteer there will tell it honestly. The Occupation was five years of ordinary people getting by, and sometimes not.
Halcrow was shifty, you say? Everyone in Lerwick is shifty in January, it is the squad rehearsals. The next lead is the Guernsey Occupation Museum. Ferry to Poole, then across.
Thread on the bench. The galley shed has a binder too, name of Halcrow, I am told. Ask him about the thread. Politely. A binder who is cross is a binder who stops.
Search the galley shed in Lerwick. The thread on the torn page was waxed linen, and that is a shed full of sailmakers and ropes. Look at the benches.

Lerwick next. The skipper of the crew in the Lounge will only talk to somebody who can pull on a rope in time. Sing with them. Ferry to Aberdeen, the Kirkwall boat, then the Lerwick boat. It is a long road. That is rather the point.

A strip with stitching holes, and a ticket stub in a pantomime script. The strip is waxed linen thread, sewn by hand. The stub is half the island's bookmarks. Keep both in the Casebook, the stub in pencil.
The Shetland section of the Roll went first. Go to Lerwick. Take the Liverpool boat, the Aberdeen boat, then north. Sing with the crew in the Lounge. They trust a voice.
Have a look round the prompt corner. Behind the prompt book. That is where the Roll lives. Lived.
The Clerk at the Tram Depot will tell you about Tynwald. He will tell you about the horses too. Listen to the first half.

else.text: Quayle. Archivist, Gaiety Theatre. Yes, the theatre keeps the archive. The island trusts actors to remember things and nobody else.

I keep the Roll of the Isles: one ledger where Mann, Shetland and the Channel Islands each write down what they say aloud once a year, so it never goes quiet. Tynwald Day. Up Helly Aa. Liberation Day.

Three sections of pages are missing from the bound Roll, one for each island. I would like them found, and I would like the Roll read out properly, at a Gathering, with all three islands in one room. That wants someone who will go and listen.
Will you go and listen for the Roll?

then.text: Not yet is fine. The Roll has waited since the year it began. Come back when you have the boots on.

else.text: Splendid. First the Clerk at the Tram Depot: Tynwald, from the Clerk who has to say it out loud every year. Then the prompt corner here, where the Roll was kept. Look behind the book.
